paras: The lynching of L. S. Elmer took place early on July 27, 1888, at Wahpeton, Dakota Territory, when a masked mob took the deputy sheriff from the Richland County jail and hanged him from the bridge over the Bois des Sioux River. Elmer was accused of having shot Mollie Korbel, a domestic in the sheriff's household, two days earlier. A coroner's jury blamed persons unknown; the local paper hailed the hanging as justice, and wire reports spread it nationally, stressing that the sheriff would not fire on the mob.

Elmer was a deputy under Sheriff Miller and boarded in his house, where Korbel, 21 and Bohemian, cooked for the deputies and the jail's prisoners. He had reportedly served as a deputy or jailer at Rochester, Austin and Fargo and been discharged for drinking.

On the evening of Wednesday, July 25, with the Miller family away, Elmer shot Korbel three times. The Wahpeton Times and the St. Paul Globe's correspondent blamed jealousy, whereas the wire said he had not been courting her and 'no cause is known'. The Times also charged that he had planned to blame Conden, a helper who found the body.

A crowd crying 'Lynch him!' gathered as Elmer was locked up, and the ringleaders of an attempt to storm the jail that night were arrested. On Thursday Korbel's body lay in state in the courtroom, Elmer waived examination before Justice Gray, and special deputies guarded the jail.

At about 1 a.m. Friday, by local accounts, some 100 masked men broke in with a battering ram, overpowered Sheriff Miller and his deputies, and battered open the cages with sledges. The Times and the Globe said Elmer twice tried to hang himself before the mob reached him; a syndicated account instead described him sitting calmly on his cot. With a noose on his neck he was hurried to the bridge before a crowd the Globe put at about 800, and asked if he wished to pray, he answered 'No.'

His last words were reported three ways: that he was glad, that he did not know why and was sorry, or that he acted 'in the heat of passion'. The body hung, watched from the bridge, until it was cut down between 4 and 5 a.m.

A coroner's inquest at Rice's undertaking rooms found that Elmer 'came to his death at the hands of persons unknown,' and Rice buried him that day. The sheriff reportedly resisted but would not shoot, saying 'the life of the murderer was not worth the life of a friend.' Business houses closed for Korbel's funeral at St. Adelbert's church on Saturday. No report of any arrest or prosecution of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The Wahpeton Times headed its report 'THE BEAST LYNCHED', wrote that 'Wahpeton manhood has risen and avenged' the murder, and ended 'A noble retribution, well done!' On August 9 it reprinted with approval a Wahpeton letter to the Globe calling the hanging a 'duty' and arguing that a jury might have found Elmer insane.

Elsewhere the story moved by wire from July 27, as 'He Paid the Penalty' in the Washington Critic and 'The Sheriff Accommodated the Lynchers' in the New York Sun. The wire stressed the 'pretty' victim, the sheriff's refusal to shoot his friends and spectators who 'went home satisfied', while garbling names into 'Slemmer' and 'Keortsel'.

Minnesota papers added notes on Elmer's past, and the New Ulm Weekly Review's narrative, later reprinted by the Times, ended 'blood atoned for blood'. Weekly summaries reduced the case to one line, and the Bossier Banner set it beside a Virginia lynching of 'A negro'.
Reports differ on the hour (1 or 2 a.m.), the deputy (Pelham or Bronte), the mob's size (about 100 or seventy-five) and the river (Bois des Sioux or Red); the local versions are closest to the event.

reader.title: Lynching of L. S. Elmer
bases: A masked crowd broke into the Richland County jail at Wahpeton, took the prisoner L. S. Elmer from the sheriff and hanged him from a river bridge (A1, A3, A5, A8).

A masked mob of about 100 (A5, A8; about 75 in A24) overpowered the sheriff and deputies, took Elmer from jail and hanged him, and the local paper presented the hanging as justice for his killing of Mollie Korbel (A1, A3); the coroner's jury found death 'at the hands of persons unknown' (A3).
The local Wahpeton Times (A1, A3), the St. Paul Globe's Wahpeton specials (A4, A8) and the Associated Press-style wire (A5, A9, A24) agree on the jail break and hanging from the bridge.

accounts.label: Wahpeton Times (local)
accounts.gist: Elmer shot Korbel from 'jealousy, spite and cussedness' and planned to blame Conden; an organized masked body of citizens broke into the jail at 1 a.m. while Elmer twice tried to hang himself, and hanged him from the Bois des Sioux bridge.

accounts.label: St. Paul Globe Wahpeton specials
accounts.gist: A jilted lover shot the girl; two days later 100 masked men broke in at 1 a.m., and Elmer, who said he 'was glad of it', was hanged at the 'Red river bridge' before about 800 cheering people.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: No cause was known for the shooting; a masked mob of 100 headed by men of Wahpeton and Breckenridge overpowered the sheriff, who would not fire on his friends; Elmer said he did not know why he killed her and was sorry.

accounts.label: 'Another account' (syndicated)
accounts.gist: Bohemian farmers withdrew to use 'strategy'; about seventy-five masked men hustled aside the sheriff and twelve deputies; Elmer sat calmly, then told the mob he killed her 'in the heat of passion' and said 'hoist away'.

accounts.label: Wahpeton correspondent to the St. Paul Globe
accounts.gist: Elmer upbraided Korbel for being civil to other men and planned a premeditated murder; citizens performed a 'duty', and a jury might have found him insane.

framing.detail: The local Wahpeton Times headed its report 'THE BEAST LYNCHED', wrote that 'Wahpeton manhood has risen and avenged' the murder, and called the hanging 'A noble retribution, well done!'
On August 9 the Times reprinted with approval a Wahpeton letter to the St. Paul Globe arguing that such a murder 'merits just such treatment'.

Distant papers ran the wire under headlines like 'He Paid the Penalty', 'Strung Up', 'The Sheriff Accommodated the Lynchers' and 'Emotional Insanity Got Choked', emphasizing the murder's atrocity and the satisfied crowd.
Weekly news summaries reduced the case to one line, the Bossier Banner pairing it with a Virginia lynching of 'A negro'.

record_check.dossier: Accused of shooting Mollie Korbel; jealousy is the local paper's motive, while the wire said no cause was known.
A masked mob of about 100 (about 75 in one account), said to be headed by men of Wahpeton and Breckenridge; not an organized standing band. The inquest named no one.

record_check.record: A man was carried from a yard ... The paper approves the hanging.
record_check.dossier: Accurate as far as it goes but omits the victim's name, the accusation and the jail break; the man was Deputy Sheriff L. S. Elmer.

info: Elmer shot Mollie Korbel on the evening of Wednesday, July 25, 1888; the mob hanged him early on Friday morning, July 27.
Taken from the jail in the sheriff's quarters at Wahpeton and hanged from the bridge over the Bois des Sioux River (one report says the 'Red river bridge').
L. S. (Lee S.) Elmer, a deputy sheriff; printed also as 'L. S. Elmar', 'L. Slemmer', 'S. S. Elmer', 'L. D. Elmer', 'Emer'. His race is not stated.

Accused of shooting and killing Mollie (also 'Mary') Korbel, 21, a domestic in Sheriff Miller's household, in the sheriff's house; motives reported variously as jealousy, her refusal of his advances or of marriage, no known cause, or 'heat of passion'.
Masked men described as well organized and 'headed by resolute men of Wahpeton and Breckenridge'; the local paper called them 'deliberate citizens'.
Body cut down by the coroner or Undertaker Rice between 4 and 5 a.m. and buried the same day.
